title: Storage Hardware
summary: How HDDs and SSDs actually store bits, why SSDs are so much faster, and why they eventually wear out.

blocks.markdown:
**Storage hardware** is the physical device that holds data when the power is off — unlike RAM, which forgets everything.

- Two dominant kinds: **HDD** (spinning magnetic disk) and **SSD** (flash chips, no moving parts).
- SSDs are replacing HDDs almost everywhere except cheap bulk storage.
- Both sit below RAM in the [memory-hierarchy](memory-hierarchy) — slower, but non-volatile and cheaper per byte.

blocks.subTitle: Platters and heads
blocks.markdown:
An **HDD (hard disk drive)** stores bits as magnetic patterns on spinning metal disks called **platters**.

- A **read/write head** on a moving arm floats just above each platter surface.
- Platters spin at a fixed speed (commonly 7200 RPM); data sits in circular **tracks**.
- To access data, the head must physically move to the right track and wait for the right spot to spin underneath it.

blocks.subTitle: Seek time and rotational latency
blocks.markdown:
Two delays make HDDs slow for random access.

- **Seek time** — time for the arm to move the head to the target track (~4-9 ms).
- **Rotational latency** — time waiting for the disk to spin the target sector under the head (~2-4 ms average).
- Both happen *before* any data transfers, so scattered small reads are far slower than one big sequential read.

blocks.subTitle: NAND flash
blocks.markdown:
An **SSD (solid-state drive)** stores bits as trapped electric charge in **NAND flash** chips — no platters, no moving parts.

- Charge presence/absence represents a bit; it holds without power.
- No seek time or rotational latency — any cell is reached electronically, so random access is fast.
- Trade-off: flash cells wear out with repeated writes (more on this later).

blocks.subTitle: Pages, blocks, and erase-before-write
blocks.markdown:
Flash is organized into **pages** (~4 KB, smallest unit you can write) grouped into **blocks** (~128-256 pages).

- You can write to an empty page directly, but you **cannot overwrite** a page in place.
- To reuse a page, the whole **block** must be erased first — this is **erase-before-write**.
- Erasing is slow and wears the cells, so SSDs avoid it on every write.

blocks.subTitle: The FTL and wear leveling
blocks.markdown:
The **FTL (flash translation layer)** is firmware inside the SSD that maps logical addresses (what the OS sees) to physical flash pages.

- On a rewrite, the FTL writes the new data to a fresh page elsewhere and marks the old page invalid, instead of erasing on the spot.
- **Wear leveling** — the FTL spreads writes evenly across all blocks so no single block wears out early.
- A background job called **garbage collection** later erases blocks full of invalid pages to reclaim space.

The core trade-off in one table.

| | HDD | SSD |
|---|---|---|
| Moving parts | Yes | No |
| Random access | Slow (ms) | Fast (µs) |
| Cost per GB | Low | Higher |

HDDs still win for cheap bulk/archival storage; SSDs win everywhere latency matters.

The **interface/protocol** connecting the drive to the CPU matters as much as the storage medium.

- **SATA** — older protocol designed for HDD speeds; one command queue, capped around 600 MB/s.
- **NVMe (non-volatile memory express)** — built for flash, talks directly over the fast **PCIe** bus, supports thousands of parallel command queues.
- An SSD on SATA is bottlenecked by the interface, not the flash — NVMe unlocks the flash's real speed.

Three storage technologies, ranked by speed and volatility.

| Tech | Volatile? | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| DRAM | Yes | Fastest |
| Flash (SSD) | No | Fast |
| Disk (HDD) | No | Slow |

**Volatile** means it loses data without power — DRAM needs constant refresh, so it's used for RAM, never permanent storage.

blocks.sectionTitle: Where storage sits in the hierarchy
blocks.markdown:
Storage sits at the bottom of the speed/cost pyramid.

Each step down trades speed for capacity and lower cost per byte. See [memory-hierarchy](memory-hierarchy) and [io-buses-interrupts](io-buses-interrupts) for how the CPU reaches these devices.

blocks.subTitle: Why SSDs wear out
blocks.markdown:
Each erase-write cycle on a flash cell slightly damages the insulating layer that traps charge.

- After enough cycles (often thousands, depending on flash type), a cell can no longer reliably hold a charge.
- Manufacturers rate drives in **TBW (terabytes written)** — total data the drive can absorb before wear becomes a risk.
- Wear leveling and garbage collection delay this, but they can't stop it — SSDs have a finite write budget.

Common mistakes:

- **"SSDs never fail."** They fail differently — by write wear, not mechanical breakdown — but they do fail.
- **"NVMe is a storage medium."** It's the interface/protocol; the flash chips are the medium. You can have SATA SSDs too.
- **"More RAM makes storage speed irrelevant."** Cold data and cache misses still hit the disk — storage speed still matters.

blocks.subTitle: HDD vs SSD
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: HDD vs SSD — what's the fundamental difference?**

HDDs store bits magnetically on spinning platters and need a physical head to seek to the data. SSDs store bits as charge in flash cells with no moving parts, so any cell is reached electronically. That's why SSDs crush HDDs on random access and are silent and shock-resistant.

blocks.subTitle: Erase-before-write and wear leveling
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why must SSDs erase before writing, and what is wear leveling?**

Flash can only flip charge one direction per page (empty to written); reusing a page needs the whole block erased first, since erasing only works at block granularity. Wear leveling is the FTL's strategy of spreading writes across all blocks evenly, so no single block hits its erase-cycle limit before the rest.

blocks.subTitle: Seek time and why random access differs
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is seek time, and why is SSD random access so much faster than HDD?**

Seek time is how long an HDD's head takes to physically move to the right track before it can even start reading. SSDs have no head and no track to seek — any address resolves to a flash location electronically in microseconds, so random reads don't pay a mechanical penalty at all.
